Identity is coordinate, and address is space.

## Overview

synTagma is a spatial coordinate space computing system. Its core primitive, [Tagma](/projects/syntagma/tagma/), is a 16-bit coordinate embedded in the Unicode Hangul syllable block (U+AC00--U+D7AF) that replaces hash-based addressing with direct structural addressing. Every valid 16-bit value is simultaneously a 1-D address (Unicode code point), a 3-D coordinate (initial, medial, final), and a displayable Hangul syllable.

The system spans two layers:

**Tagma (core primitive).** The atomic coordinate: a 16-bit value with closed-form composition, three independent axes, zero collision probability, and single-cycle combinational decoding. A variable-length syllable sequence extends the address space from $1.1 \times 10^4$ to $2^{256}$ while keeping lookup cost linear in syllable count.

**synTagma coordination system** The recursive and distributed extension of the Tagma arithmetic across physical topologies. A synTagma coordinate at recursion level $k$ is a Cartesian product of three Tagma syllable sequences at level $k-1$:

$$\mathbb{T}_k = \mathbb{T}_{k-1} \times \mathbb{T}_{k-1} \times \mathbb{T}_{k-1}$$

Each axis of a recursive coordinate can reside on a different physical node. A topology mapping function $\phi_k$ assigns axes to nodes; the recursive linearisation formula produces the same index regardless of how axes are distributed. No distributed consensus is required because each axis is independently stored and independently accessed.

## Tagma core primitive

The core Tagma coordinate is defined by the Hangul composition formula (ISO/IEC 10646):

$$C(i,m,f) = \text{U+AC00} + 588i + 28m + f, \quad 0 \leq i < 19,\; 0 \leq m < 21,\; 0 \leq f < 28$$

Of 65,536 representable 16-bit states, 11,172 satisfy this formula. The remaining 54,364 are structurally invalid and hardware-detectable. Each valid value is:

- A 1-D address (Unicode code point) for flat array indexing
- A 3-D coordinate (initial, medial, final) for structural queries
- A Hangul syllable for human-readable display

The core library provides several data structures built on the Tagma coordinate:

- A fixed-size bit array supporting bitwise set operations over the full coordinate space.
- A direct-address table mapping each valid single-syllable coordinate to an associated value; lookup is a single index computation with no hashing.
- A multi-level tree for storing values indexed by variable-length syllable sequences; allocation is demand-driven, and each level uses the same direct-address mechanism.
- A variable-depth trie for sequences whose length is determined at runtime rather than compile time.

All of these structures resolve collisions by construction: the coordinate space guarantees that distinct values produce distinct indices.

Full documentation: [Tagma primitive page](/projects/syntagma/tagma/).

## Coordination layer

The coordination layer extends Tagma's arithmetic to physical topologies without modifying the core. Its components:

**Recursive coordinate space.** The composition formula admits unbounded $k$ levels of recursion. A 19-syllable sequence at $k=0$ occupies the SHA-256 scale; at $k=1$ each of its three axes is itself a full 19-syllable sequence, producing $S_1 \approx 7.30 \times 10^{231}$ distinct addresses. Access follows the recursive linearisation formula:

$$\text{index}(a,b,c) = a \cdot S_{k-1}^2 + b \cdot S_{k-1} + c$$

**Physical topology mapping.** The three axes of a recursive coordinate need not reside on the same device. The topology function $\phi_k: \{i,m,f\} \rightarrow \mathcal{N}$ assigns each axis to a physical node. Axes on the same node are resolved locally; axes on different nodes require transport. The assignment is a deployment parameter determined by data locality and fault isolation.

**Axis fungibility.** The coordinate axes carry no intrinsic semantics at the protocol level. The same resolver procedure, transport format, and consistency model apply whether axis 0 represents "region", "shard", or "timestamp". This separation between coordinate algebra and axis interpretation allows routing across heterogeneous topologies without modifying the core arithmetic.

**Self-routing.** A syllable sequence carries its own address. Given a sequence and current recursion depth, any node determines whether each sub-axis is local or remote by applying $\phi_k$. No separate routing table lookup is required.

**Consistency.** Resolution requires no distributed consensus. Each axis is independently stored and independently accessed. The linearisation formula is a pure function of independent axis values, so cross-node reads require no coordination. Write operations affecting different axes target independent address subspaces on different nodes.

## Performance

Based on a software reference implementation, measured lookup latency: 0.38 ns vs 227 ns for SHA-256 (597x) at single-syllable; 54.9 ns vs 227 ns (4.1x) at SHA-256 scale (19 syllables). Structural prefix queries show the decisive advantage: Tagma answers nonexistent prefix in 1.65 ns while a general-purpose hash table scans 10M entries in 23.05 ms (14.0Mx). See benchmarks section in [Tagma](/projects/syntagma/tagma/wp.html#sec-appendix-benches) Whitepaper: All measured on Apple M1 with [cargo bench code](https://github.com/ssccsorg/syntagma/blob/main/sw/rust/benches/bench.rs).

Cross-validation from hardware verification: the [Ibex RV32IMCB Exhaustive Verification Report](/projects/ev/ibex.html#performance-structural-enumeration-vs-standard-pipeline) using ev (ExaVerif) confirms the same structural advantage on real RISC-V instruction encoding spaces. synTagma-based structural enumeration verifies 524,288 combinations in 49.5 ms versus 3.63 s for the standard pipeline (73x), and at 2M scale reaches 846x by eliminating runtime constraint evaluation entirely. The verification covers the full lowRISC Ibex core ALU decode logic. See the full [Ibex RV32IMCB Exhaustive Verification Report](/projects/ev/ibex.html) for details.
